strengths: The paper offers a genuinely novel inversion of the intrinsic-dimensionality methodology (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021): instead of fixing data and varying the model, it fixes the model and varies the reasoning strategy in the training data, providing a quantitative, MDL-grounded lens on why some CoT variants generalize better.

The experimental design is thoughtful about fairness: a common absolute accuracy threshold is enforced across strategies (with a clear justification for why percentage-based thresholds from prior work are inappropriate here), and the results are shown robust to threshold choice (Table 3), model size (1B vs 4B), and in-distribution vs out-of-distribution evaluation.

The choice of baseline metrics is well-motivated and the comparison is informative: trajectory length, sequence KL divergence, and token perplexity are all tested, and the analysis of why KL divergence fails (length confound) and why perplexity is related but weaker is coherent and consistent with Yue et al. (2025).

The authors address an obvious confound (training set size varies across strategies, 6.2K-7.5K) and show it is uncorrelated with downstream accuracy (rho ~ -0.11, p > 0.7), with the notable counterexample that Executed PoT has the fewest examples yet the best performance.

The qualitative findings are interesting beyond the headline correlation: Executed PoT achieving both lowest intrinsic dimension and best OOD accuracy, larger models compressing effective strategies better while requiring more capacity for ineffective ones, and the useful practical note that intrinsic dimension can be computed from training curves alone without validation or OOD data.
Writing is generally clear; the appendix provides reproducible details (LoRA sweep algorithm, hyperparameter selection, dataset sources, per-strategy examples).
weaknesses: Scope of evidence is narrow relative to the generality of the claims: all conclusions rest on a single task (GSM8K) and two models from a single family (Gemma-3 1B/4B). The title and abstract state a general claim ('effective reasoning chains reduce intrinsic dimensionality'), but no evidence is provided that this holds for other domains (symbolic reasoning, knowledge tasks, other datasets) or other model families, despite the paper itself citing evidence that CoT benefits are highly task-dependent.

The core result is a Spearman rank correlation computed over only n=14 data points. While the correlations are statistically significant and consistent across models (0.93/0.75), confidence intervals at this sample size are wide, and the margin over token perplexity (0.82/0.63) rests on very few observations. No confidence intervals or permutation tests are reported for the difference between intrinsic dimensionality and the perplexity baseline.

The intrinsic-dimension measurement itself is coarse and noisy: it is estimated from only k=20-30 log-spaced LoRA configurations, and the reported values (e.g., 1.03, 1.49, 2.05, 3.92, 7.34M) show heavy discretization/ties. The relationship between 'number of trainable LoRA parameters' and true intrinsic dimension of the objective is only approximate, and structured choices about which modules receive LoRA (attention vs MLP) could systematically interact with reasoning format in unexamined ways.

There is a potential circularity in the measure: intrinsic dimensionality is computed from training accuracy of the same fine-tuning pipeline whose generalization is being predicted. Strategies that are intrinsically easier to fit may simply be formats closer to the base model's prior (indeed, the authors acknowledge the interrelation with perplexity), so the metric may partially re-encode 'distributional closeness' rather than providing an independent explanation. The paper discusses the connection but does not disentangle it experimentally.

The epoch-1-based threshold is pragmatic but somewhat ad hoc: training accuracy after one epoch conflates format learnability, sequence length, and convergence speed; the paper asserts this 'isolates the learnability of the reasoning structure' without direct evidence for that interpretation.

The evaluation protocol for PoT strategies on OOD stress tests is underspecified: models fine-tuned to emit code presumably require an interpreter at test time on GSM-Symbolic/GSM-IC/GSM-Hard, but this is never stated, and it materially affects whether Executed PoT's OOD numbers are comparable to natural-language strategies.

The work is strictly correlational, yet the discussion drifts toward causal language ('effective reasoning chains facilitate learning by better compressing the task'), which the evidence does not establish (e.g., no intervention showing that reducing intrinsic dimension causes better generalization).
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many nontrivial implementation details (teacher-model prompting, filtering, sweep configuration, evaluation harness).

The computational cost of the metric is high (dozens of full fine-tuning runs per strategy), which the authors acknowledge; the practical utility of the metric is therefore limited, and no cheaper surrogate is proposed.

strengths: The central idea is interesting and clearly articulated: fix the model, vary the reasoning strategy in the training data, and measure how many trainable parameters (via LoRA rank/module sweeps) are needed to reach a fixed accuracy threshold. This inverts the standard intrinsic-dimension setup (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021) in a sensible way and connects it to MDL-style reasoning about why CoT helps.

The evaluation is reasonably systematic: 14 reasoning strategies spanning length, structure, distractors, and code-based approaches, evaluated on both ID (GSM8K) and multiple OOD stress tests (GSM-Symbolic, GSM-IC, GSM-Hard), with results for two model sizes (Gemma-3 1B and 4B).

The comparison against baseline metrics (trajectory length, token perplexity, sequence KL) is a useful meta-evaluation, and the distractor-based strategies (Short CoT with n distractors) provide a controlled manipulation showing the metric degrades predictably as reasoning structure degrades.

The robustness analysis over threshold selection (Table 3) and the discussion of why epoch-1 training accuracy avoids memorization contamination are thoughtful, and the paper is honest about the relationship between intrinsic dimensionality and token perplexity and about the computational cost of the measure.

Appendices provide useful detail: the LoRA configuration selection algorithm, dataset sizes, verification that training set size does not correlate with performance, and worked examples of every strategy.
weaknesses: Extremely narrow empirical scope for the breadth of the claims. All evidence comes from a single dataset (GSM8K grade-school word problems) and a single model family (Gemma-3) at two small scales. The abstract and conclusion frame intrinsic dimensionality as a general quantitative measure of reasoning effectiveness, but there is no evidence it transfers to other task types (symbolic, knowledge-intensive, multi-step agentic) or other model families. The title-level claim is much broader than what is shown.

A significant potential confound is not disentangled: the reasoning strategy is entangled with output format regularity. Executed PoT achieves the lowest intrinsic dimensionality, but code is a highly repetitive, deterministic, low-entropy format that the base model already knows well; low training loss with few parameters may reflect output-format simplicity or computation offloading to the interpreter (arithmetic is no longer learned in weights), rather than 'effective reasoning compresses the task.' The paper's own observation that intrinsic dimension and token perplexity are interrelated (0.82/0.63 correlations) points to exactly this concern, but no experiment isolates format regularity from reasoning quality (e.g., scrambled CoT controls, or code with distractor comments).

The causal/MDL interpretation is loose. LoRA rank times number of adapted matrices is a coarse, architecture-dependent proxy for 'description length' or 'degrees of freedom,' and the parameter counts are quantized on a log-spaced sweep of only k=20/30 configurations. The resulting intrinsic dimension values are coarse and heavily tied (e.g., many strategies share 1.49M, 2.05M, 7.34M), which undermines fine-grained rank comparisons and the precision implied by reporting values like 0.93.

Statistical treatment is thin. Correlations are computed over only 14 strategies; no seed variance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for the underlying fine-tuning runs, no uncertainty on the intrinsic dimension estimates themselves, and no test of whether the difference between intrinsic dimensionality's correlation (0.93) and token perplexity's (0.82) is meaningful at n=14. Strategies that never reach the threshold are censored at full capacity, which further distorts the correlation.

The threshold construction has a mild circularity: tau is derived from the maximum epoch-1 training accuracy achieved by any strategy, and training accuracy at threshold crossing is measured on data that includes strategy-specific output formats; it is unclear how 'training accuracy' is even computed for Executed PoT (does it require executing generated code?), which is central to the headline result.

Several important experimental details that affect interpretation are missing or unclear: number of training seeds per configuration, variance across LoRA sweep configurations at the same parameter count (only one config per target count is kept), how validation checkpoints are selected without leaking into the ID/OOD comparison, and no release of code or data-generation prompts to support reproducibility of the teacher-generated training sets.

Novelty is modest: the measurement apparatus is directly inherited from Li et al. (2018), Aghajanyan et al. (2021), and LoRA, and the finding that PoT outperforms CoT on GSM8K is well established (Sprague et al., 2025). The contribution is the reframing plus the correlation analysis, which is a useful but incremental empirical observation.

The paper has an limitations-adjacent discussion but does not confront the main threats to validity (single task, format confound, censorship at full capacity); presentation also contains multiple typos and loosely worded claims (e.g., 'its predicts', 'Emprically', 'the MDL principle suggestions that').

strengths: The central idea is a clean and clever inversion of the intrinsic dimension literature (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021): rather than fixing data and varying the model, the authors fix the model and vary the supervision (reasoning strategy), using LoRA sweeps as a structured low-dimensional projection to estimate the task's intrinsic dimension. This provides a genuinely novel, quantifiable lens on what makes reasoning chains effective.

The experimental design is unusually thorough for a correlational study: 14 diverse reasoning strategies spanning baselines, teacher CoTs, code-based approaches, and distractor variants; two model scales (Gemma-3 1B and 4B); in-distribution and multiple out-of-distribution test splits; and a generalization check on Reasoning Gym tasks outside mathematics.

The threshold-selection concern is well anticipated and addressed: Section 4.3 and Table 3 show conclusions are robust across thresholds (70%, 80%, 90% of epoch-1 train accuracy, and 90% of validation accuracy), and the epoch-1-based threshold avoids overfitting contamination and enables computing the metric from training curves alone — a nice practical property.

The comparison against plausible alternative metrics (trajectory length, token perplexity, sequence KL divergence, and even LongPPL variants in Appendix D) strengthens the claim that intrinsic dimensionality has superior predictive power (0.93 vs. 0.82 for perplexity on 4B; 0.75 vs. 0.63 on 1B).

Useful secondary analyses: the correctness ablation (Table 5) showing incorrect chains inflate intrinsic dimensionality by 125–500x with corresponding accuracy drops, the dataset-size confound check in Appendix B.1 (no significant correlation between training set size and accuracy), and the observation that effective strategies compress better in larger models while ineffective ones reverse the pattern.

The MDL/information-theoretic grounding in Section 5 is appropriate and the paper is generally well written, with limitations (computational expense of the metric, LoRA-based upper bounds) honestly discussed in Section 6 and the impact statement.
weaknesses: The evidence is correlational on a small sample (n=14 strategies for the main GSM8K results), and the abstract and conclusion drift toward causal language ('effective reasoning chains facilitate learning by better compressing the task') that the design cannot support. No intervention (e.g., editing chains while holding correctness/length fixed) is performed to establish that intrinsic dimensionality is a mechanism rather than a correlate.

The incremental value over token perplexity is not clearly established. Perplexity already achieves 0.82 (4B) and 0.63 (1B), and the authors themselves argue the two metrics are 'potentially interrelated.' No partial correlation, residual analysis, or joint model is reported to show intrinsic dimensionality predicts generalization beyond what perplexity captures — given that perplexity is far cheaper to compute, this is the key practical question and it remains open.

The measurement has notable coarseness: intrinsic dimensions in Table 1 cluster on a small set of discrete values (1.49M, 2.05M, 3.92M, 532.81M, etc.) because the greedy configuration search produces few unique parameter counts, so many strategies share ranks; no confidence intervals or variability across training seeds/runs are reported for the sweep, despite the threshold-crossing point on step-function-like curves being sensitive to run-to-run noise.

The Reasoning Gym validation (Table 4) is weak: each category uses only 4 strategies, and a Spearman correlation of 1.00 on 4 points carries essentially no evidential weight, particularly in the cognitive category where the best strategy is No CoT. This limits the claimed generality beyond math.

Scope is narrow for a main-track empirical claim: one model family (Gemma-3), one primary dataset (GSM8K), LoRA-only parameterization (which the authors concede is only an upper bound on intrinsic dimension), and fine-tuning from teacher-generated chains only. Whether the metric transfers to RL-based post-training, larger models, or other domains is left to future work.

Some experimental choices are under-justified: the derivation of tau from the maximum epoch-1 training accuracy 'by any strategy' means the reference point is set by the strongest strategy, which could systematically advantage strategies whose curves rise early; and the LoRA sweep uses a fixed training step budget whose interaction with parameter count (small adapters may need more steps) is not analyzed.
No code or data release is mentioned, which is a reproducibility concern given the metric depends on many fine-tuning sweeps and a specific configuration-selection algorithm.

strengths: The paper poses a clear, well-motivated question (what makes a reasoning strategy effective?) and offers a quantitative, falsifiable answer grounded in the intrinsic-dimension/MDL literature. The experimental inversion — fixing the model and varying the training data via reasoning strategy — is a clean and novel use of the intrinsic dimension methodology of Li et al. (2018) and Aghajanyan et al. (2021).

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this type of analysis: 14 reasoning strategies spanning baselines, distractor-perturbed CoTs, PoT variants, and prior-work strategies; two model scales (Gemma-3 1B and 4B); five OOD stress-test splits plus GSM8K; a threshold-robustness analysis (Table 3); a data-correctness ablation (Table 5); generalization to Reasoning Gym tasks (Table 4); and careful baseline comparisons including token perplexity, sequence KL, length, and LongPPL (Table 7).

The robustness analysis in Section 4.3 directly addresses the most obvious objection — arbitrariness of the threshold τ — and shows correlations remain stable (0.72–0.94) across four threshold choices, which strengthens confidence that the finding is not a hyperparameter artifact.

The confound control is partially thoughtful: Appendix B.1 shows training-set size does not correlate with downstream accuracy (ρ ≈ −0.11, p > 0.7), and the 'No CoT with extra tokens' baseline helpfully separates filler-token effects from reasoning quality. The appendix provides concrete examples of every strategy, and the limitations (computational cost of the sweep, LoRA as a loose upper bound on ID) are honestly discussed.

The headline result — Spearman correlation of 0.93 (4B) and 0.75 (1B) between intrinsic dimensionality and overall generalization, substantially exceeding perplexity (0.82/0.63), KL divergence (−0.17/−0.18), and length (0.31/0.24) — is replicated across model scales and is consistent with an independently motivated prediction from MDL theory.
weaknesses: The intrinsic dimensionality estimates are heavily quantized and the metric's resolution is a serious concern. The sweep contains only k=20–30 LoRA configurations distributed in log space over ~4 orders of magnitude, and the reported d_int values show extensive ties (e.g., 1.49M, 2.05M, 2.55M, 3.92M shared across many top strategies in Table 1; 1.03M, 7.34M, 31.45M shared in Table 2). Spearman correlations computed on 14 rank values with this degree of tying, without confidence intervals, seed variance, or any per-strategy uncertainty on d_int, are fragile; the reported p < 0.01 significance likely understates the true uncertainty. Rank ordering within the top cluster of strategies (which carries much of the correlation) may not be reliable.

The 'intrinsic dimension' is computed from a monotone envelope (Pareto frontier) of training accuracy vs. parameter count. Training accuracy of a single LoRA run at a fixed step count is a noisy quantity, and taking the monotone upper envelope systematically biases curves upward; no repeated runs are reported to quantify run-to-run variance in the crossing point. Without error bars, differences of one or two grid points between strategies are uninterpretable.

Potential confounds are acknowledged but not fully ruled out. Effective chains (e.g., Short CoT, Executed PoT) tend to contain the computation that produces the answer, so the final answer is largely copied from context rather than computed — low d_int may partly reflect answer leakage/format simplicity rather than 'compressibility of the underlying mapping.' The strong correlation of token perplexity (0.82) with d_int's 0.93 suggests the two metrics may be measuring largely the same phenomenon, but the correlation between the metrics themselves is never reported, so the claimed added value of intrinsic dimensionality over perplexity is not cleanly established.

The external-validation evidence is statistically weak. Table 4 has n=4 strategies per category, where a Spearman correlation of 1.00 is trivially attainable and carries essentially no evidential weight; the cognitive category even shows the inverse pattern (No CoT best). Presenting these as confirmation overstates the generality beyond GSM8K-style arithmetic.

The central claim is correlational, and the paper's framing occasionally slides beyond what the evidence supports (e.g., 'effective reasoning chains facilitate learning by better compressing the task'). With one task family dominating (GSM8K), 14 data points, and a single model family, the claim that intrinsic dimensionality is a general quantitative measure of reasoning effectiveness is plausible but not yet demonstrated; a broader task or model-family sweep would be needed.

Practical utility is limited and only partially acknowledged: computing d_int requires training the model across a full LoRA sweep up to near-full capacity on the very data whose quality is being assessed, so the metric cannot be used to cheaply pre-screen reasoning data before committing training compute. The paper admits this in the conclusion, but the introduction's framing (informing data annotation and alignment) oversells it.

No code release or clear reproducibility statement is provided. Given that the entire contribution hinges on a specific sweep procedure (greedy configuration selection, threshold computation, epoch-1 accuracy), the absence of released code or seeds notably weakens reproducibility.

Minor presentation issues: Figure 1 is cluttered and hard to parse; the Reasoning Gym section reports correlations on 4 points without flagging their limited power; and Table 1's footnote on significance marking does not clarify how ties were handled in the Spearman computation.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reframing: the paper inverts the standard intrinsic-dimension methodology (Li et al., 2018; Aghajanyan et al., 2021) by fixing the model and varying the data through reasoning strategies, connecting CoT effectiveness to the MDL/compression view of generalization.

Broad and careful empirical design: 14 diverse reasoning strategies spanning length, structure, distractors, and code-based approaches; two model scales (Gemma-3 1B/4B); both in-distribution and multiple OOD stress-test splits; plus a transfer experiment on Reasoning Gym tasks.

Good control experiments: robustness of conclusions across threshold choices (Table 3), an ablation on training-data correctness (Table 5), a check that training-set size does not drive the correlations, and comparisons against multiple baseline metrics including LongPPL variants (Appendix D).

Honest limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges the computational cost of the metric, that LoRA provides only an upper bound on intrinsic dimensionality, and that perplexity may be interrelated with the proposed measure.
Clear presentation with a helpful overview figure (Figure 1) and intuitive Pareto-frontier visualizations (Figures 2 and 3) that make the intrinsic-dimension computation transparent.
weaknesses: The core evidence is correlational with small sample sizes: Spearman correlations are computed over only 14 strategies (GSM8K) and just 4 strategies per Reasoning Gym category. With n=4, the reported correlations of 1.00 (and the unstable -1.00 for token PPL) carry essentially no statistical weight, so the domain-generalization claims (Section 4.5) are weakly supported.

Potential confounding with base-model perplexity is acknowledged but not disentangled: token perplexity achieves 0.82 correlation, and low-intrinsic-dimension strategies also have low PPL. A partial-correlation or matched-pair analysis isolating intrinsic dimensionality from base-model likelihood is missing, leaving open whether the paper's metric is largely re-measuring 'in-distribution-ness' of the teacher data.

The intrinsic-dimension estimates are heavily quantized by the LoRA sweep design (only four module groups x integer ranks), producing repeated values (e.g., 1.49M, 2.05M, 3.92M appear many times). Several strategies share identical measured intrinsic dimensions yet differ substantially in accuracy, which limits the metric's resolution and the strength of the claimed 'strong predictor' role.

The causal framing ('effective reasoning chains facilitate learning by better compressing the task') goes beyond the evidence. Data that is easier to fit also generalizes better for well-understood reasons, so some of the observed relationship is close to expected; the paper would benefit from a sharper test that distinguishes its compressibility hypothesis from generic learnability effects.

No error bars, seeds, or variance reporting for the training runs underlying the Pareto frontiers; training accuracy at a single checkpoint is noisy, and rank-crossing points on a coarse sweep are sensitive to this noise.

Generality is limited: the main results are on GSM8K and its variants (with a small Reasoning Gym extension), on a single model family, and with teacher-generated data from one instruction-tuned model. Whether the ordering holds for genuinely different task families or other model families is not demonstrated.

The paper does not state whether code or generated datasets will be released, which matters for reproducibility given the substantial compute involved in the sweeps and the many bespoke strategy datasets.
